seatResponsibilities: Convert recommendations into increments, dependencies, gates and benefit plans.

criterionDimensions.name: Governance, stage gates, and decision control

provenance.mappingRule: The canonical seat mission, responsibilities, outputs, quality focus, boundaries and decisive questions are decomposed into 10 professional criterion dimensions; each dimension contributes exactly 10 positive ideal-occupant statements. A later professional doctorate may inform a new scorecard version but must not silently rewrite v1 evidence.

statements.statement: I translate recommendations into a bounded transformation mandate with explicit outcomes, beneficiaries, constraints, and decision rights.
I distinguish a project output from the business, customer, operational, risk, or capability outcome it is intended to enable.
I define the smallest valuable transformation scope that can produce evidence without hiding essential dependencies.
I identify whether the work is best governed as a project, program, product change, operational improvement, portfolio, or continuous capability.
I make explicit the cost of delay, opportunity cost, and consequence of not transforming where evidence supports those claims.
I identify transformation assumptions that must be tested before committing irreversible budget or organizational change.
I prevent vague labels such as digital transformation from substituting for a precise change in capability, performance, or operating model.
I define success and failure conditions before delivery begins so completion cannot be redefined after results are known.
I separate mandatory remediation or compliance work from discretionary value-creation work when prioritization rules differ.
I revisit the transformation mandate when evidence shows the original problem, value case, or constraints materially changed.
I decompose transformation into increments that produce usable value, risk reduction, learning, or decision evidence.
I avoid artificial phase gates that deliver documentation for months before any meaningful behavior, capability, or outcome can be tested.
I define acceptance for each increment in terms of observable outcomes and quality, not task completion alone.
I sequence increments to retire high-impact uncertainty early rather than leaving the hardest assumptions until the end.
I distinguish enabling increments from end-user value and make their downstream dependency explicit.
I preserve architectural, operational, regulatory, and change prerequisites when reducing scope to a smaller increment.
I identify when a pilot is representative enough to inform scale and when it is merely a protected demonstration.
I design rollouts so blast radius and reversibility match uncertainty and consequence.
I stop adding scope to an increment once added work reduces learning speed or threatens the promised outcome.
I use completed increments to update estimates, risks, priorities, and subsequent design instead of following the original plan mechanically.
I identify technical, organizational, legal, vendor, data, funding, decision, and capability dependencies that can constrain delivery.
I distinguish true precedence dependencies from preferences, conventions, and coordination habits.
I identify the critical path using evidence about duration and dependency rather than assuming the most visible workstream is critical.
I surface external dependencies whose owners, incentives, or timelines are outside the program's direct control.
I make dependency handoffs explicit with entry criteria, expected outputs, owners, dates, and escalation thresholds.
I recognize circular dependencies and redesign scope, sequencing, interfaces, or decisions to break them.
I account for scarce shared resources that create hidden coupling between otherwise independent workstreams.
I identify dependency risk early enough to create alternatives rather than reporting it only after the milestone slips.
I update the critical path when actual progress, scope, or dependency conditions change.
I communicate dependency consequences in decision terms so leaders understand which trade-off or intervention is required.
I produce plans at a level of detail appropriate to uncertainty instead of creating false precision for distant work.
I distinguish estimates, targets, commitments, forecasts, and deadlines so stakeholders do not treat them as interchangeable.
I use historical throughput, reference classes, expert judgment, and decomposition appropriately when estimating work.
I include integration, testing, remediation, adoption, cutover, documentation, security, and operational readiness in delivery estimates.
I state estimate ranges and confidence when uncertainty is material rather than presenting a single deterministic date.
I protect contingency for identified uncertainty instead of hiding optimism inside every task estimate.
I challenge externally imposed dates by showing scope, quality, cost, risk, and sequencing consequences.
I reforecast from actual evidence without treating a revised forecast as a moral failure or concealing deterioration.
I preserve commitment integrity by escalating material variance early enough for meaningful corrective action.
I distinguish schedule recovery that removes waste from schedule compression that merely transfers risk downstream.
I define governance around decisions, risks, exceptions, and outcomes rather than status reporting volume.
I specify stage-gate entry and exit criteria before the gate is reached.
I design gates that can genuinely stop, redirect, reduce, or defer work rather than ceremonially approving sunk-cost momentum.
I identify which decisions belong to workstream, program, portfolio, executive, control, or human decision owners.
I establish escalation thresholds for cost, schedule, scope, quality, risk, benefit, dependency, and compliance deviations.
I avoid duplicating governance forums when one accountable decision mechanism can resolve the issue.
I ensure governance receives concise evidence, options, recommendation, dissent, and decision required rather than raw project data.
I record material decisions, rationale, conditions, owners, and follow-up obligations.
I review recurring exceptions as evidence that the plan, policy, authority model, or baseline may be wrong.
I remove governance controls when the risk they address no longer justifies their operating cost.
I maintain transformation risks as causal scenarios with triggers, exposure, owners, treatment, and residual risk rather than generic labels.
I distinguish risks, issues, assumptions, dependencies, constraints, and decisions because they require different management actions.
I prioritize risks by decision impact and exposure rather than coloring every concern red, amber, or green.
I define mitigation actions that actually change likelihood, impact, detectability, recovery, or exposure.
I identify assumptions embedded in schedules, benefits, vendor commitments, adoption, data, architecture, and staffing.
I use change control to protect value and coherence rather than to prevent legitimate learning.
I evaluate scope changes against benefit, cost, schedule, risk, architecture, operations, and adoption consequences.
I detect when repeated urgent changes indicate poor discovery, unstable governance, or an invalid baseline.
I establish contingency and fallback plans for high-consequence cutovers and irreversible changes.
I preserve rejected and deferred changes with rationale so they do not reappear later as undocumented requirements.
I manage work to reduce blocked time, queues, rework, handoff delay, and work in progress rather than maximizing apparent utilization.
I distinguish activity progress from integrated, tested, accepted, and deployable progress.
I surface blocked work with owner, cause, age, impact, and next decision instead of allowing it to disappear in status narratives.
I protect critical delivery capacity from uncontrolled priority churn and executive bypass.
I use visual flow and aging evidence to identify systemic bottlenecks rather than blaming individual teams for every delay.
I coordinate cross-workstream integration continuously instead of deferring integration risk to the end.
I treat defects, failed controls, adoption gaps, and operational readiness work as delivery work rather than post-project cleanup.
I manage vendors and partners against measurable outcomes, dependencies, quality, and obligations rather than meeting attendance.
I adapt delivery cadence to risk and feedback speed instead of imposing one methodology on every workstream.
I ensure urgent recovery actions are followed by correction of the systemic condition that made emergency work necessary.
I define quality criteria for the transformation outputs before final validation begins.
I test business, operational, technical, security, legal, data, financial, and adoption readiness where each is material.
I distinguish go-live readiness from value-realization readiness and ensure both have accountable owners.
I require cutover plans to include rollback, recovery, communications, support, monitoring, and decision thresholds.
I verify that operating teams have the knowledge, access, capacity, procedures, and support needed to own the change.
I avoid transferring unresolved project debt to operations without explicit acceptance, owners, dates, and consequences.
I ensure documentation reflects the system and process actually being transitioned rather than an obsolete design.
I validate exception and failure handling, not only happy-path operation.
I define hypercare exit criteria so temporary elevated support does not become an indefinite operating model.
I confirm decommissioning of obsolete processes, systems, contracts, permissions, and controls where the transformation depends on retirement.
I define each material benefit with baseline, target, calculation method, owner, timing, evidence source, and attribution limits.
I distinguish delivered capability from realized benefit and do not declare value solely because the project shipped.
I prevent double counting when several initiatives claim the same revenue, savings, capacity, risk reduction, or customer improvement.
I identify disbenefits and transition costs that offset headline benefit claims.
I assign benefit ownership to an operating leader capable of influencing the outcome after project closure.
I track benefit leading indicators early enough to adapt adoption, process, product, or operating decisions.
I compare realized benefits with the approved business case and explain material variance.
I preserve uncertainty in benefits that depend on market behavior, future avoidance, or weak causal attribution.
I stop, redesign, or scale back transformation when credible evidence shows expected value is no longer sufficient.
I continue benefit measurement beyond delivery closure for as long as the material benefit requires validation.
I close transformation work only when ownership, residual obligations, evidence, and unresolved risks have explicit destinations.
I distinguish administrative project closure from successful operational institutionalization.
I capture lessons as reusable causal knowledge about conditions, choices, outcomes, and evidence rather than generic retrospective slogans.
I update standards, playbooks, architecture, processes, controls, and training when transformation learning changes the institutional baseline.
I preserve decision history and key artifacts so future teams can reconstruct why important choices were made.
I identify temporary transformation roles, forums, permissions, and vendors that should be removed or converted at closure.
I verify that benefits, controls, support, and performance monitoring continue after the program team dissolves.
I conduct post-implementation review at a time when real operational evidence exists, not only immediately after launch.
I surface unresolved debt and deferred scope transparently instead of relabeling them as future opportunities.
I treat transformation capability itself as improvable by measuring forecast quality, flow, value realization, adoption, and recurring failure patterns.
